opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the obstacle isn't one thing. It's that every part of the stack breaks at once when you go that far.

The most obvious one is compute and memory. With standard attention, cost grows quadratically with length, and even with linear or sparse variants, the KV cache alone becomes absurd at a trillion tokens. You can't hold it on any realistic cluster. So you're forced into some kind of compression, retrieval, or hierarchical memory. Once you do that, the question becomes: what do you throw away, and who decides? That's really a modeling question, not just an engineering one.

The second obstacle, which I think people underestimate, is data. Where do you get natural training signal that actually requires a trillion tokens of context? Almost no real task has dependencies spanning that far. If you just concatenate documents, the model learns that distant context doesn't matter, because it usually doesn't. So you need tasks, maybe synthetic, maybe agentic, where something learned early is genuinely needed much later. Otherwise the model will never learn to use the long context, even if the architecture supports it.

Third is credit assignment and optimization. Even if you can run the forward pass, backpropagating through that span isn't feasible end to end. So you end up with truncated gradients, chunked training, or some memory-writing mechanism trained with a different objective. Then you have to ask whether the model actually learns *what* to remember, or whether you've just built a very expensive cache.

And finally, evaluation. Needle-in-a-haystack tests are easy to saturate and don't tell you much. We don't yet have good ways to measure whether a model truly reasons over a huge history rather than just looking things up.

So if I had to pick the key obstacle, I'd say it's this: we don't yet know what the right inductive bias for memory is. Is it attention over everything, or something closer to how humans work, compressing experience into knowledge and only occasionally retrieving specifics? I lean toward the second. A trillion-token context probably shouldn't look like a giant window at all. It should look more like a model that keeps learning as it goes.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that training is possible if genuinely trillion-length training contexts are available.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret continued decreases in training loss as evidence that the model is learning to compress contexts.

r003.rationale: The response notes a lack of natural training signal for dependencies spanning a trillion tokens, but identifies the right inductive bias for memory as the key obstacle—not constructing genuinely trillion-length contexts.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think the key obstacle is the one people usually name first, which is compute. Compute is a real constraint, but it's the kind of constraint that engineering steadily erodes. The deeper problem is that we don't actually know how to make a model *care* about something that happened a trillion tokens ago.

Let me unpack that a bit. When we went from four thousand to a hundred thousand to a million tokens, the architecture mostly stayed the same. We changed position encodings, we did some continued pretraining on long data, we made attention cheaper. But the model was still fundamentally a thing that reads the whole context and attends over it. At a trillion tokens, that framing just breaks. You cannot attend over a trillion tokens, and even if you could, almost all of it is irrelevant to any given prediction. So the question becomes: what do you keep, what do you compress, what do you throw away, and who decides?

And that's where it gets hard, because the decision has to be made before you know what question will be asked later. Humans do this all the time. You read a book, you forget most of the sentences, but you retain the structure, the surprises, the things that contradicted what you believed. We don't have a good training signal for that in language models. Next-token prediction rewards local fluency. It doesn't reward remembering the one line on page 200 that matters on page 90,000.

So the obstacle, in my view, is the data and the objective, not the hardware. Where do you get naturally occurring sequences of a trillion tokens where long-range dependency genuinely matters, and how do you build a loss that punishes the model for forgetting the right things? If you can't answer those, you can scale the context window as far as you like and the model will mostly ignore it. You'll get a very expensive model with a very short effective memory.

The second thing I'd mention, which is related, is evaluation. Needle-in-a-haystack is basically a retrieval test, and models already game it. What we don't have is a benchmark where a model has to accumulate understanding over a huge span and then act on it. Until we can measure that, we can't really train for it, because we won't know whether our tricks are working or just making the loss curve look nice.

r001.rationale: The response asks where to get relevant trillion-token sequences, but does not state that the capability can be trained if such contexts are available.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret declining training loss as evidence that the model is learning to compress contexts.

r003.rationale: It calls data and the training objective key obstacles and specifically asks where to get naturally occurring trillion-token sequences with meaningful long-range dependencies.

astra-6.text: I think the key obstacle is getting the model to actually use that context, rather than simply making it possible to feed in that many tokens. Computation and memory are enormous constraints, of course. But even if we solve those, we still need training data and objectives that require the model to connect information across very long distances. If it can answer by looking only at a small local window, it has little incentive to learn that capability. So the challenge is both efficient computation and a training signal that makes the long context necessary.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key obstacle is making that context useful, not simply making it fit. Even if we solve the memory and computation problems, we still need to train the model to find relevant information across an enormous sequence and connect it reliably. That raises a difficult question: what training data and learning signal will actually teach it to use such distant context? Increasing the context window alone doesn’t guarantee that ability.
